name: Hiroki Haraguchi
bio: Proposed metallomics as an integrated field for studying metals and metal-containing biomolecules. His foundational 2004 paper connects elemental analysis and chemical speciation with the questions raised by genomics and proteomics.
affiliation: Nagoya University · Nagoya, Japan
bioParagraphs: Proposed metallomics as an integrated field for studying metals and metal-containing biomolecules. His foundational 2004 paper connects elemental analysis and chemical speciation with the questions raised by genomics and proteomics.

impact.headline: Gave metals a place beside genes and proteins
impact.discovery: Haraguchi proposed metallomics as a field integrating the study of metals with genomics and proteomics. His foundational paper made chemical speciation central: identifying the metal-containing molecules that perform biological work, rather than treating an elemental measurement as a complete account of metal biology.
impact.significance: This is the organizing idea behind microbial metallomics. A microbial gene inventory cannot establish which metal-dependent reactions are operating. Haraguchi’s framework asks researchers to connect elements, their molecular partners, and biological function—the bridge needed between microbiome sequencing and a chemically informed account of health or exposure.
impact.frontier: The continuing challenge is to measure metal-containing molecules in complex microbial communities while preserving their chemical identities and linking those measurements to expressed biological functions.

sources.label: Haraguchi, Metallomics as integrated biometal science (2004)

name: Robert J. P. Williams
bio: Helped establish bioinorganic chemistry and the Irving–Williams stability series. His work connected metal coordination, enzyme function and biological evolution, providing a chemical foundation for understanding why cells use particular elements.
affiliation: University of Oxford · Oxford, UK
bioParagraphs: Helped establish bioinorganic chemistry and the Irving–Williams stability series. His work connected metal coordination, enzyme function and biological evolution, providing a chemical foundation for understanding why cells use particular elements.

impact.headline: Explained the chemical competition behind metal selection
impact.discovery: Williams helped establish how metal coordination governs biological function. With Harry Irving, he described a recurring order of stability among transition-metal complexes. His work connected such chemical preferences to metalloenzymes, making the identity and binding environment of a metal central to explanations of catalysis.
impact.significance: This foundation explains why having enough metal is insufficient: a competing element may bind where another is needed. Microbial metallomics therefore has to examine chemical competition and cellular control together. Mismetallation becomes a mechanistic question about an enzyme’s occupancy and activity, rather than a vague claim of metal toxicity.
impact.frontier: The next step in applying this foundation is to establish which proteins acquire the wrong metal under real exposure conditions, and whether that change impairs function.

sources.label: Irving and Williams, The stability of transition-metal complexes (1953)
Royal Society scientific profile

name: Barry P. Rosen
bio: Studies how organisms transport, transform and detoxify arsenic and other metals. His work on arsenic uptake, efflux, biomethylation and organoarsenical chemistry links bacterial resistance mechanisms to environmental exposure. FIU records his retirement in 2025.
affiliation: Florida International University · Miami, USA
bioParagraphs: Studies how organisms transport, transform and detoxify arsenic and other metals. His work on arsenic uptake, efflux, biomethylation and organoarsenical chemistry links bacterial resistance mechanisms to environmental exposure. FIU records his retirement in 2025.

impact.headline: Made arsenic exposure a question of cellular handling
impact.discovery: Rosen’s work maps how organisms admit, export, and transform arsenic. With colleagues, he demonstrated that the bacterial glycerol channel GlpF also permits entry of trivalent arsenic and antimony, while a separate transport system supports their removal. Environmental contamination thus meets specific cellular pathways, not an inert biological surface.
impact.significance: For microbial metallomics, this turns a total arsenic result into a set of consequential questions: which chemical species is present, which organisms encounter it, and how do they handle it? His research connects environmental exposure to microbial physiology and helps explain why resistance, accumulation, and toxicity are different outcomes.
impact.frontier: An important frontier is determining how these cellular pathways collectively alter arsenic speciation and host exposure in intact communities, where competing transformations may occur simultaneously.

sources.label: FIU research profile
Meng, Liu and Rosen, Arsenic and antimony transport (2004)

name: Marc Solioz
bio: Investigated the copper-handling cop operon in Enterococcus hirae, including the CopY repressor, CopZ chaperone and CopA/CopB ATPases. This work helped connect copper transport, intracellular delivery and gene regulation. The linked publication documents his research at Bern.
affiliation: University of Bern · Bern, Switzerland
bioParagraphs: Investigated the copper-handling cop operon in Enterococcus hirae, including the CopY repressor, CopZ chaperone and CopA/CopB ATPases. This work helped connect copper transport, intracellular delivery and gene regulation. The linked publication documents his research at Bern.

impact.headline: Connected copper delivery to bacterial gene control
impact.discovery: Solioz helped turn copper homeostasis into a connected molecular system through work on Enterococcus hirae. A collaborative study showed that the copper chaperone CopZ delivers copper to the CopY regulator, changing its association with DNA. Copper routing could therefore be linked directly to the regulation of copper-handling genes.
impact.significance: His contribution explains how a microbe interprets and responds to a metal exposure. The biological effect depends on intracellular delivery and regulation as well as the amount outside the cell. That distinction is essential when studying copper contamination, copper-containing materials, or differences in microbial tolerance.
impact.frontier: The field now needs to connect these molecular responses to mixed communities and realistic exposure histories, rather than inferring ecological outcomes from a single organism’s tolerance.

sources.label: Cobine and colleagues, Copper delivery from CopZ to CopY (1999)
Solioz and Stoyanov, Copper homeostasis in Enterococcus hirae (2003)

name: Nigel J. Robinson
bio: Leading theorist of protein "metalation" — how cells ensure each metalloprotein gets the correct metal — and of metal-sensing regulators such as the nickel sensor InrS.
affiliation: Durham University · Durham, UK
bioParagraphs: Leading theorist of protein "metalation" — how cells ensure each metalloprotein gets the correct metal — and of metal-sensing regulators such as the nickel sensor InrS.

impact.headline: Made available metal quantitatively distinguishable from total metal
impact.discovery: Robinson and colleagues used bacterial metal sensors to define the intracellular availability of different elements in thermodynamic terms. Comparing those values with a protein’s metal affinities explained how a cobalt-requiring enzyme can receive cobalt even when other metals bind more tightly in isolated biochemical measurements.
impact.significance: This supplies a quantitative foundation for the atlas’s central distinction: a metal can be present without being available to a particular protein. It also makes mismetallation testable. The relevant comparison is between competing intracellular metal pools and protein affinities, rather than between dietary dose and a presumed biological effect.
impact.frontier: A major frontier is extending calibrated measurements of metal availability across species and physiological states, then testing whether they predict protein occupancy in complex host-associated communities.

sources.label: Osman and colleagues, Bacterial sensors and correct enzyme metalation (2019)

name: David P. Giedroc
bio: Investigates how bacteria sense and manage metals, reactive sulfur species and oxidative stress. His laboratory combines structural biology, spectroscopy and biochemistry to explain the regulatory switches that keep essential metal chemistry under control.
affiliation: Indiana University Bloomington · Bloomington, USA
bioParagraphs: Investigates how bacteria sense and manage metals, reactive sulfur species and oxidative stress. His laboratory combines structural biology, spectroscopy and biochemistry to explain the regulatory switches that keep essential metal chemistry under control.

impact.headline: Revealed how metal binding becomes a regulatory signal
impact.discovery: Giedroc’s research explains the molecular switches by which bacteria respond to metals. Work on the zinc sensor CzrA showed that zinc changes the protein’s internal motions and weakens DNA binding, even without a dramatic overall structural change. Metal detection is therefore a dynamic communication process within a protein.
impact.significance: His work fills the gap between a metal entering a cell and that cell changing its behavior. For microbial metallomics, knowing that a metal binds is insufficient: researchers must establish whether binding triggers the correct response. That distinction helps explain why metal balance depends on functional regulation.
impact.frontier: The translational question is whether metal-sensing responses can be altered selectively enough to have useful biological effects, while accounting for different regulatory systems in host and community members.

sources.label: Capdevila and colleagues, Entropy redistribution in a metalloregulatory protein (2017)
Giedroc Group, Indiana University

name: Amy C. Rosenzweig
role: Professor of Molecular Biosciences and Chemistry
bio: Investigates metalloprotein function with structural, spectroscopic, biochemical and genetic methods. Major interests include biological methane oxidation, oxygen activation, metal uptake and transport, and the biosynthesis of metal-binding natural products.
affiliation: Northwestern University · Evanston, USA
bioParagraphs: Investigates metalloprotein function with structural, spectroscopic, biochemical and genetic methods. Major interests include biological methane oxidation, oxygen activation, metal uptake and transport, and the biosynthesis of metal-binding natural products.

impact.headline: Shows metal enzymes working in their biological surroundings
impact.discovery: Rosenzweig’s group connects metalloprotein structure with chemical function. In a study of bacterial methane oxidation, examining particulate methane monooxygenase in a lipid environment restored activity and revealed previously unresolved structural features, including a copper-binding site. The work showed how the surrounding membrane can change the interpretation of an enzyme.
impact.significance: This matters beyond one copper enzyme: microbial metal function cannot always be reconstructed from an isolated protein stripped of its surroundings. Her work links metal chemistry to microbial carbon cycling and provides a standard for validating function before making claims about environmental activity or a proposed biological application.
impact.frontier: A continuing challenge is to establish metal occupancy and catalytic behavior in intact organisms and communities, where membranes, metal supply, and environmental conditions act together.

sources.label: Koo and colleagues, Active methane monooxygenase in a lipid bilayer (2022)
Northwestern research profile

name: Valeria C. Culotta
bio: Investigates how metals and reactive oxygen species shape the interaction between hosts and fungal pathogens. Her laboratory studies copper, manganese, iron and superoxide dismutases, with particular attention to Candida albicans and Candida auris.
affiliation: Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health · Baltimore, USA
bioParagraphs: Investigates how metals and reactive oxygen species shape the interaction between hosts and fungal pathogens. Her laboratory studies copper, manganese, iron and superoxide dismutases, with particular attention to Candida albicans and Candida auris.

impact.headline: Showed that infection changes metal geography
impact.discovery: Culotta and colleagues demonstrated that copper availability changes during experimental Candida infection and that the fungus adjusts its antioxidant enzymes accordingly. In the mouse model, rising serum copper did not describe the changing copper conditions in infected kidneys. The organism switched between copper- and manganese-dependent forms of superoxide dismutase.
impact.significance: Her work makes a crucial point explicit: a blood metal measurement need not report the environment experienced by a microbe in tissue. It also shows why nutritional immunity is dynamic. A pathogen’s metal requirements and defenses can change during infection, complicating simple assumptions about supplementing or withholding one element.
impact.frontier: The next clinical bridge is to measure these local metal states and fungal responses during human infection, then determine which findings predict meaningful treatment outcomes.

sources.label: Li and colleagues, Candida adaptation to host copper (2015)
Johns Hopkins, Culotta Lab

name: Thomas V. O'Halloran
bio: Investigates the cell biology and coordination chemistry of metals, including intracellular metal trafficking, zinc dynamics and copper homeostasis. His work on metallochaperones helped explain how cells deliver reactive metal ions to the proteins that need them.
affiliation: Michigan State University · East Lansing, USA
bioParagraphs: Investigates the cell biology and coordination chemistry of metals, including intracellular metal trafficking, zinc dynamics and copper homeostasis. His work on metallochaperones helped explain how cells deliver reactive metal ions to the proteins that need them.

impact.headline: Established that metals require directed intracellular delivery
impact.discovery: O’Halloran and collaborators helped establish the metallochaperone concept. Their work on the yeast protein Atx1 identified a soluble copper receptor that interacts with a copper-trafficking partner. This supplied a molecular explanation for how cells can route a reactive, potentially toxic ion toward the proteins that need it.
impact.significance: The contribution changes what metal sufficiency means. Copper entering a cell does not guarantee that it reaches the appropriate destination. Microbial metallomics must therefore examine delivery pathways as well as transport and total abundance—a principle that connects nutrient utilization, cellular dysfunction, and the interpretation of metal exposure.
impact.frontier: A key frontier is determining when altered trafficking, rather than altered total copper, explains a biological phenotype and how that distinction can be measured reliably.

sources.label: Pufahl and colleagues, Atx1 copper chaperone function (1997)
O’Halloran laboratory publication record

name: Deborah B. Zamble
bio: Investigated how bacteria acquire and deliver nickel to enzymes, including the metallochaperones involved in hydrogenase maturation. Her work helped explain the coordination between metal sensing, transport and enzyme assembly. This historical entry commemorates her contributions.
affiliation: University of Toronto · Toronto, Canada
bioParagraphs: Investigated how bacteria acquire and deliver nickel to enzymes, including the metallochaperones involved in hydrogenase maturation. Her work helped explain the coordination between metal sensing, transport and enzyme assembly. This historical entry commemorates her contributions.

impact.headline: Explained how bacteria select and deliver nickel
impact.discovery: Zamble’s research established molecular connections among bacterial nickel sensing, acquisition, and enzyme maturation. Her group studied how nickel-delivery proteins recognize the metal and interact with one another, including work on the changing nickel-binding environments of the hydrogenase maturation proteins HypA and HypB. Nickel utilization emerged as a coordinated cellular process.
impact.significance: Her contribution is fundamental to understanding why nickel exposure affects organisms differently. An enzyme’s dependence on nickel does not mean all nickel in its surroundings can activate it. The sensing and delivery machinery helps determine usable supply, giving microbial metallomics a functional explanation beyond simply listing nickel-dependent species.
impact.frontier: The continuing question is how nickel delivery operates under the chemical constraints of real host niches, and whether that knowledge supports selective, validated therapeutic approaches.

sources.label: University of Toronto, scientific remembrance of Deborah Zamble
Lacasse and colleagues, Nickel binding by HypA (2019)

name: Kevin J. Waldron
role: Professor of IBB PAS; Head of Laboratory
bio: Studies how metalloproteins acquire the correct metal and how metal specificity evolves. Current laboratory work includes superoxide dismutases, bacterial metal homeostasis and the consequences of metal starvation for enzyme function.
affiliation: Polish Academy of Sciences (IBB) · Warsaw, Poland
bioParagraphs: Studies how metalloproteins acquire the correct metal and how metal specificity evolves. Current laboratory work includes superoxide dismutases, bacterial metal homeostasis and the consequences of metal starvation for enzyme function.

impact.headline: Showed why metal deprivation can meet metabolic flexibility
impact.discovery: Waldron and collaborators demonstrated that a Staphylococcus aureus antioxidant enzyme can function with either iron or manganese. Their biochemical and infection-model evidence connected this cofactor flexibility to survival during host-imposed manganese restriction. The work explains an organism’s response to nutritional immunity at the level of enzyme function.
impact.significance: This is important for microbiome medicine because an organism’s metal requirement may be conditional. Lowering one metal does not necessarily remove the function that depends on it under ordinary conditions. Waldron’s work makes metabolic flexibility part of evaluating metal-directed interventions and interpreting microbial responses to an inflamed environment.
impact.frontier: A next step is establishing how widespread functional cofactor flexibility is in host-associated communities, and when it changes responses to metal deprivation in clinically relevant settings.

sources.label: Garcia and colleagues, Cofactor flexibility and nutritional immunity (2017)
IBB PAS, Laboratory of Metalloprotein Biology

name: Amit R. Reddi
bio: Investigates the cellular mechanisms that activate metalloproteins and regulate their signaling functions. His laboratory focuses on heme trafficking and copper/zinc superoxide dismutase, using chemical biology to connect metal availability with metabolism and disease.
affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology · Atlanta, USA
bioParagraphs: Investigates the cellular mechanisms that activate metalloproteins and regulate their signaling functions. His laboratory focuses on heme trafficking and copper/zinc superoxide dismutase, using chemical biology to connect metal availability with metabolism and disease.

impact.headline: Made mobile heme pools visible inside cells
impact.discovery: Reddi and colleagues developed fluorescent sensors that distinguish exchangeable heme from the larger total heme pool. In yeast, these tools revealed different heme availability across cellular compartments and linked a familiar metabolic protein, GAPDH, to heme buffering. Heme could be studied as a dynamic resource as well as an enzyme cofactor.
impact.significance: This gives microbial metallomics a way to ask what a cell can actually use. A total iron or heme measurement cannot establish availability at a particular destination. Reddi’s measurement tools help connect metal allocation to metabolism and signaling, which is necessary for separating abundance from functional sufficiency.
impact.frontier: The next question is how exchangeable heme changes across host-associated organisms and stress states, and which measurements can link those changes to specific biological outcomes.

sources.label: Hanna and colleagues, Fluorescent sensors reveal heme dynamics (2016)
Georgia Tech research profile

name: Christopher Rensing
bio: Studies metal–microbe interactions across environmental and medical settings. His research connects bacterial metal resistance with electromicrobiology and bioremediation. ASM identifies him as a distinguished professor and director of the Institute of Environmental Microbiology at FAFU.
affiliation: Fujian Agriculture & Forestry University · Fuzhou, China
bioParagraphs: Studies metal–microbe interactions across environmental and medical settings. His research connects bacterial metal resistance with electromicrobiology and bioremediation. ASM identifies him as a distinguished professor and director of the Institute of Environmental Microbiology at FAFU.

impact.headline: Identified transport mechanisms that turn exposure into tolerance
impact.discovery: Rensing, Mitra, and Rosen demonstrated that the bacterial protein ZntA uses cellular energy to transport zinc and cadmium. This work connected metal tolerance to a defined transport function. Rensing’s broader research carries that mechanistic perspective across environmental microbiology, metal resistance, and the biological handling of contaminated environments.
impact.significance: His contribution makes exposure assessment more biologically specific. Organisms sharing the same metal-containing environment may maintain different intracellular burdens because their transport systems differ. For microbial metallomics, that helps explain ecological selection and why external metal concentration alone cannot establish either microbial injury or the fate of a contaminant.
impact.frontier: The frontier is connecting measured transport activity to community changes under realistic mixtures and exposure durations, including determining when tolerance changes environmental metal mobility.

sources.label: Rensing, Mitra and Rosen, ZntA metal transport (1997)
American Society for Microbiology profile

name: Dietrich H. Nies
bio: Investigates how bacteria maintain metal balance in highly contaminated environments. Work with Cupriavidus metallidurans and its metal-efflux systems has helped explain how microbes tolerate metals and transform their surrounding chemistry.
affiliation: Martin-Luther-University Halle-Wittenberg · Halle, Germany
bioParagraphs: Investigates how bacteria maintain metal balance in highly contaminated environments. Work with Cupriavidus metallidurans and its metal-efflux systems has helped explain how microbes tolerate metals and transform their surrounding chemistry.

impact.headline: Made mixed-metal toxicity a mechanistic problem
impact.discovery: Nies and colleagues studied how Cupriavidus metallidurans survives metal-rich environments and transforms gold compounds. Their work showed that copper and gold can interact toxically because gold interferes with copper export. The biological response to a mixture therefore differed from what separate measurements of either metal would suggest.
impact.significance: This is a direct reason to take environmental metallomics seriously: one contaminant can disturb the handling of another element. Nies’s work connects microbial tolerance, metal transformation, and mixture effects. It provides a mechanistic basis for asking what contamination does to microbial function, beyond documenting that metals are present.
impact.frontier: The next challenge is determining which mixture interactions matter at environmental concentrations and how microbial transformation changes exposure over time in soils, water, and other communities.

sources.label: Wiesemann and colleagues, Copper–gold mixture toxicity (2017)
Bütof and colleagues, Copper–gold detoxification and biomineralisation (2018)

name: John D. Helmann
bio: Uses Bacillus subtilis to study cellular responses to metal deficiency, metal excess, reactive oxygen species and antibiotics. His laboratory examines transcriptional regulation and the molecular sensors that coordinate these stress responses.
affiliation: Cornell University · Ithaca, USA
bioParagraphs: Uses Bacillus subtilis to study cellular responses to metal deficiency, metal excess, reactive oxygen species and antibiotics. His laboratory examines transcriptional regulation and the molecular sensors that coordinate these stress responses.

impact.headline: Revealed that microbes reorganize their metal budgets
impact.discovery: Helmann’s work connects metal-sensing regulators to coordinated physiological responses. In Bacillus subtilis, studies of zinc-responsive ribosomal proteins showed how alternative proteins help sustain growth during zinc scarcity. The ribosome participates in the metal economy: a cell can change how it allocates zinc while preserving essential protein synthesis.
impact.significance: For microbial metallomics, this explains why a change in metal supply can alter cellular priorities before it stops growth. Taxonomic abundance alone may miss that transition. Helmann’s research directs attention to resource allocation and stress responses when interpreting what nutritional immunity or environmental metal scarcity is doing to a community.
impact.frontier: A useful next step is to track metal allocation and expressed functions alongside community composition, establishing which adaptations remain active in complex, changing environments.

sources.label: Gabriel and Helmann, Zinc-responsive ribosomal proteins (2009)
Cornell research profile

name: Katherine J. Franz
role: James B. Duke Distinguished Professor of Chemistry
bio: Investigates how biological systems manage the coordination chemistry of essential but potentially toxic metals, especially copper and iron. Her laboratory develops chemical tools to change metal location, speciation and reactivity, including approaches relevant to microbial pathogens.
affiliation: Duke University · Durham, USA
bioParagraphs: Investigates how biological systems manage the coordination chemistry of essential but potentially toxic metals, especially copper and iron. Her laboratory develops chemical tools to change metal location, speciation and reactivity, including approaches relevant to microbial pathogens.

impact.headline: Connected metal availability to antifungal drug response
impact.discovery: Franz and colleagues showed in laboratory Candida cultures that exposure to fluconazole changes the organism’s sensitivity to copper availability. Their chemical analyses distinguished this biological interaction from simply forming a copper–drug complex. The result links an established antifungal drug’s effects to the metal conditions surrounding the treated cells.
impact.significance: This points to a concrete opportunity for metallomics in medicine: the chemical environment can influence how a drug performs. Franz’s work gives researchers a way to examine metal–drug interactions mechanistically, including location and speciation, before assuming that adding a metal or a chelator will improve treatment.
impact.frontier: The next translational question is whether these interactions persist in infected tissues with acceptable host safety and demonstrable clinical benefit; laboratory growth effects alone cannot establish that.

sources.label: Hunsaker and Franz, Copper and azole antifungal activity (2019)
Duke research profile

name: Lucia Banci
bio: Uses structural biology and NMR to study metal ions, protein maturation and intracellular metal trafficking. Her group developed in-cell NMR approaches that allow proteins to be examined in living cells at atomic resolution.
affiliation: University of Florence · Florence, Italy
bioParagraphs: Uses structural biology and NMR to study metal ions, protein maturation and intracellular metal trafficking. Her group developed in-cell NMR approaches that allow proteins to be examined in living cells at atomic resolution.

impact.headline: Observed metalloprotein maturation inside living cells
impact.discovery: Banci and colleagues developed in-cell NMR approaches that resolve protein chemistry within living human cells. In work on superoxide dismutase 1, they followed zinc binding, protein assembly, and copper uptake at atomic resolution. This made metal-dependent maturation observable in the cellular setting where the protein actually functions.
impact.significance: Her contribution helps close a central measurement gap: detecting an element and detecting a protein do not prove that the protein contains the right metal or has matured correctly. The methods offer microbial metallomics and host metal biology a way to test functional metalation rather than infer it.
impact.frontier: The frontier is extending such measurements to more proteins and physiologically relevant conditions, so altered metalation can be distinguished from changes in protein abundance or total metal.

sources.label: Banci and colleagues, Protein maturation in live human cells (2013)
CERM scientific profile

name: Caryn E. Outten
role: Professor; Guy F. Lipscomb Professor of Chemistry
bio: Studies how cells sense and distribute iron, with an emphasis on iron–sulfur clusters and glutaredoxin proteins. Her research connects the chemistry of these cofactors with iron regulation, redox balance and cellular stress.
affiliation: University of South Carolina · Columbia, USA
bioParagraphs: Studies how cells sense and distribute iron, with an emphasis on iron–sulfur clusters and glutaredoxin proteins. Her research connects the chemistry of these cofactors with iron regulation, redox balance and cellular stress.

impact.headline: Explained how iron-containing cofactors report cellular iron status
impact.discovery: Outten’s research links iron–sulfur cluster handling to the regulation of iron metabolism. Work in yeast established molecular details of cluster exchange between glutaredoxin–BolA proteins and the iron regulator Aft2. This connects the assembly and movement of an iron-containing cofactor with the cell’s decision to mobilize more iron.
impact.significance: The implication for microbial metallomics is that iron sensing is integrated with iron utilization. A cell’s response cannot be understood solely from its total iron content. Outten’s work connects cofactor delivery, redox biology, and nutrient regulation, providing mechanisms for studying functional iron disruption in microbial and host cells.
impact.frontier: A continuing question is when disrupted cluster handling produces an apparent cellular iron need despite available iron, and how to distinguish that state from simple scarcity.

sources.label: Li and Outten, Iron–sulfur cluster exchange and Aft2 (2019)
University of South Carolina research profile

name: James A. Imlay
bio: Studies how reactive oxygen species damage bacteria and how cells defend themselves. His work connects oxidative stress with iron-containing enzymes, metal availability and the repair or protection of vulnerable metabolic pathways.
affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign · Urbana, USA
bioParagraphs: Studies how reactive oxygen species damage bacteria and how cells defend themselves. His work connects oxidative stress with iron-containing enzymes, metal availability and the repair or protection of vulnerable metabolic pathways.

impact.headline: Demonstrated how the wrong metal disables metabolism
impact.discovery: Imlay and Gu showed that oxidative stress can remove iron from bacterial enzymes, after which zinc occupies the vacated sites and supports little activity. The proteins need not be destroyed for metabolism to fail. Their experiments made mismetallation a demonstrated mechanism connecting oxidative stress, competing metals, and enzyme dysfunction.
impact.significance: This is why mismetallation matters to the field. An essential nutrient can become harmful in the wrong molecular position, and the same exposure may act differently when oxidative stress changes the competition. Imlay’s work provides a concrete alternative to treating every metal-associated effect as generalized toxicity or deficiency.
impact.frontier: The next challenge is identifying which enzymes are mismetallated in real host-associated communities and linking their altered occupancy to function at relevant exposure levels.

sources.label: Gu and Imlay, Superoxide-induced mismetallation (2013)
Imlay Lab research overview

name: Lena J. Daumann
role: W3 Professor & Chair of Bioinorganic Chemistry
bio: A leader in lanthanide microbiology; characterized how methylotrophic and methanotrophic bacteria use rare-earth elements as catalytic cofactors in methanol dehydrogenase.
affiliation: Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf · Düsseldorf, Germany
bioParagraphs: A leader in lanthanide microbiology; characterized how methylotrophic and methanotrophic bacteria use rare-earth elements as catalytic cofactors in methanol dehydrogenase.

impact.headline: Expanded the biological periodic table to rare-earth chemistry
impact.discovery: Daumann’s work examines why certain bacteria use lanthanides in alcohol-metabolizing enzymes. Her group compared how different lanthanide ions affect a bacterial methanol dehydrogenase, linking differences in catalytic activity to the elements’ coordination chemistry. Closely related rare-earth elements proved biologically distinguishable rather than interchangeable members of one chemical category.
impact.significance: Her contribution broadens what microbial metallomics must look for. Elements with no established human nutritional requirement can still support microbial metabolism and environmental carbon cycling. That matters when interpreting emerging contaminants or microbial community function: the human nutrient list is not a complete map of biologically consequential metals.
impact.frontier: An important frontier is connecting enzyme-level lanthanide preferences to metal availability and metabolic activity in natural communities, especially where human activity changes rare-earth exposure.

sources.label: Lumpe and colleagues, Lanthanide identity and methanol dehydrogenase activity (2018)
HHU Bioinorganic Chemistry laboratory

name: Joseph A. Cotruvo Jr.
bio: Studies how bacteria recognize, acquire and use rare-earth elements. Research on the lanthanide-binding protein lanmodulin links microbial metal selectivity with protein engineering and opportunities for biological rare-earth separation.
affiliation: Pennsylvania State University · University Park, USA
bioParagraphs: Studies how bacteria recognize, acquire and use rare-earth elements. Research on the lanthanide-binding protein lanmodulin links microbial metal selectivity with protein engineering and opportunities for biological rare-earth separation.

impact.headline: Turned microbial metal selectivity into a separation principle
impact.discovery: Cotruvo and colleagues discovered lanmodulin, a bacterial protein that recognizes lanthanides with striking selectivity over calcium. Subsequent collaborative work demonstrated rare-earth recovery from mixtures using the protein. The research connects a microorganism’s ability to discriminate among elements with practical approaches to detecting and recovering strategically important metals.
impact.significance: This is a concrete example of microbial metallomics producing useful chemistry beyond clinical medicine. Understanding how organisms select scarce elements can inform resource recovery and environmental measurement. It also demonstrates why metal-binding specificity deserves direct study: chemically similar or abundant competing ions need not have equivalent biological access.
impact.frontier: The frontier is translating molecular selectivity into robust recovery and sensing systems for variable real-world materials, while evaluating performance, reuse, and environmental costs at larger scales.

sources.label: Cotruvo and colleagues, Discovery of lanmodulin (2018)
Deblonde and colleagues, Rare-earth extraction using lanmodulin (2020)

name: Stéphane L. Benoit
bio: Investigates nickel acquisition, storage and nickel-dependent enzymes in bacterial pathogens. His work on Helicobacter and Campylobacter connects hydrogenase and urease biology with host colonization, respiratory metabolism and iron–sulfur protein maturation. He has also explored nickel chelation against multidrug-resistant enteric bacteria in laboratory and animal-model studies.
affiliation: University of Georgia · Athens, USA

works.title: Helicobacter pylori stores nickel to aid its host colonization
Nickel chelation therapy as an approach to combat multi-drug resistant enteric pathogens
Copper toxicity towards Campylobacter jejuni is enhanced by the nickel chelator dimethylglyoxime

bioParagraphs: Investigates nickel acquisition, storage and nickel-dependent enzymes in bacterial pathogens. His work on Helicobacter and Campylobacter connects hydrogenase and urease biology with host colonization, respiratory metabolism and iron–sulfur protein maturation. He has also explored nickel chelation against multidrug-resistant enteric bacteria in laboratory and animal-model studies.

impact.headline: Turning bacterial nickel dependence into an antimicrobial target.
impact.discovery: Benoit and colleagues showed that dimethylglyoxime (DMG), a nickel chelator, inhibited growth of tested multidrug-resistant Salmonella Typhimurium and Klebsiella pneumoniae strains. Separate mouse and insect experiments supplied evidence of biological benefit. A Campylobacter jejuni study showed that metal interactions can change the antimicrobial response. These findings give experimental grounding to the idea that access to an enzyme cofactor can be a therapeutic research target.
impact.significance: His work connects the chemistry of an enzyme cofactor with the urgent search for antimicrobials. A pathogen’s metal-dependent functions can reveal targets that its conventional antibiotic-resistance profile does not describe. This is a central promise of microbial metallomics: understanding the chemistry a microbe relies on can suggest a new way to alter its behavior. Benoit and colleagues supplied experimental grounding for pursuing that direction.
impact.frontier: The next research question is where nickel-directed approaches offer a useful and selective effect in the biological settings that matter. Explaining which aspects of metal handling predict response—and which predict failure—would turn a promising proof of concept into a more informative therapeutic strategy. Host effects and the wider microbial community belong in that explanation from the beginning.

sources.label: Benoit et al. (2019) — Nickel chelation therapy as an approach to combat multi-drug resistant enteric pathogens
Benoit & Maier — DMG and copper toxicity in Campylobacter jejuni (2022)

spotlight.title: DMG shows why the mechanism deserves attention

rows.setting: Tested enteric bacterial strains · laboratory studies
rows.finding: DMG was bacteriostatic against tested Salmonella Typhimurium and Klebsiella pneumoniae, including multidrug-resistant strains. Nickel-dependent enzyme activities were inhibited.
rows.meaning: Growth inhibition and reduced enzyme activity connect metal access to bacterial function: a starting point for a different antimicrobial strategy.

rows.finding: Separate mouse experiments reported improved survival and lower organ burdens in Salmonella infection. Preventive insect experiments reported protection against the tested multidrug-resistant Salmonella and Klebsiella.
rows.meaning: The biological benefit extends beyond a culture dish and gives the therapeutic concept a reason to advance into further investigation.

rows.finding: DMG inhibited growth. Its combination with copper was bactericidal under the tested conditions; the combined effect did not generalize to selected other Gram-negative bacteria.
rows.meaning: Metal interactions can change the outcome. Organism-specific responses create an opportunity to explain when the same chemical intervention behaves differently.

spotlight.contextTitle: Why this belongs in the antimicrobial-resistance conversation
spotlight.context: WHO’s 2024 list prioritizes defined pathogen–resistance combinations for research and investment. Benoit’s work belongs in that conversation because it investigates a different therapeutic concept: restricting access to a cofactor that bacterial functions require. The findings provide a starting point for asking how widely that principle applies. The WHO list establishes the public-health priority; the biochemical and infection studies below establish the mechanistic rationale.

mechanisticCase.title: Where nickel biology meets WHO research priorities
mechanisticCase.intro: Several organisms represented in the WHO list have published nickel-enzyme biology relevant to this question. These selected examples connect a public-health priority with a biochemical or infection finding; they are not a complete enzyme census, and the cited studies do not all examine the specific resistant strains named by WHO.
mechanisticCase.caption: Published starting points for a nickel-directed antimicrobial hypothesis

rows.finding: Nickel-dependent urease activity and bacterial growth were inhibited in the DMG study, including work with multidrug-resistant isolates.
rows.question: An existing proof of concept connects nickel restriction with loss of a bacterial function.

sources.label: Benoit et al. (2019)

rows.finding: Respiratory hydrogen use was linked to virulence in a mouse study. The later DMG study reported inhibition of nickel-dependent hydrogenase activity.
rows.question: Metal access connects an energy pathway to infection biology, providing a reason to investigate nickel-directed approaches.

sources.label: Maier et al. (2004)
Benoit et al. (2019)

rows.finding: The characterized glyoxalase I was most active with nickel and inactive with zinc; other metals also supported activity in biochemical assays. Human glyoxalase I uses zinc.
rows.question: Different metal activation creates a rationale for investigating selective disruption of bacterial methylglyoxal detoxification. Nickel exclusivity in a host is a further question.

sources.label: He et al. (2000)

rows.finding: PAO1 contains three characterized glyoxalase I homologs: two in the Ni/Co-activated class and one in the zinc-dependent class.
rows.question: Multiple metal-activation classes make this an informative case for asking whether alternative enzyme activity changes the response to nickel restriction.

sources.label: Sukdeo & Honek (2007)

rows.finding: Urease, an established nickel-dependent enzyme, contributed to acid-response physiology and persistent kidney infection in mice.
rows.question: A metal-dependent function is connected to persistence in a host: a rationale for investigating nickel access in that setting. This study did not test DMG.

sources.label: Zhou et al. (2019)

sections.title: The mechanism is the reason to investigate
paragraphs: If an infection-relevant function needs nickel, and an intervention restricts the nickel pool that supplies it, that function may become a therapeutic vulnerability even when conventional antibiotics fail. This is the research hypothesis. Benoit’s work matters because it connects that biochemical idea with observed antimicrobial effects.

A chelator’s affinity is part of the argument. Biological activity also depends on which nickel pool it can reach and how that pool supplies the relevant enzyme. Restricting access during enzyme assembly is a different proposition from extracting nickel already bound inside an active enzyme. Following those connections is how microbial metallomics turns a chemical property into a biological explanation.

sections.title: An enzyme name starts the question
paragraphs: “Glyoxalase I positive” is not synonymous with nickel-dependent: distinct metal-activation classes exist. Likewise, the nickel-bearing hydrogenases are the [NiFe] class; other hydrogenase classes use iron without nickel. Enzyme presence, its actual cofactor, its activity in a host, and its contribution to infection are separate links in the argument.

A metabolic function can matter for stress survival or persistence without already having been established as a virulence factor in every organism. Identifying that missing connection is valuable foundational science. It gives a promising idea a specific next question instead of treating the absence of a completed chain as a reason to stop.

sources.label: Sukdeo & Honek (2007) — Glyoxalase I metal classes
Caserta et al. (2023) — Assembly of a [NiFe]-hydrogenase active site
Peters et al. (1998) — An iron-only hydrogenase structure

sections.title: What would move the explanation forward?
paragraphs: The mechanistic prediction is a relationship between altered nickel availability, reduced activity of the proposed nickel-dependent function, and a meaningful biological effect. A response explained equally well by unrelated toxicity would support a different account. A relevant function sustained through another metal or pathway would help explain limited response. These alternatives make the hypothesis more informative.

The larger opportunity is to connect pathogen biology, the host’s metal regulation, and the surrounding community. A community’s metal-handling functions may reveal dependencies that a species list or an antibiotic-resistance label leaves invisible. Establishing which of those dependencies matter is a research agenda for microbiome medicine—and a reason these pioneers deserve attention.

name: Eric P. Skaar
bio: Investigates the struggle between hosts and pathogens for essential nutrients. His laboratory studies bacterial metal acquisition, the action of host metal-binding proteins such as calprotectin, and the metabolic adaptations that support infection.
affiliation: Vanderbilt University Medical Center · Nashville, USA
bioParagraphs: Investigates the struggle between hosts and pathogens for essential nutrients. His laboratory studies bacterial metal acquisition, the action of host metal-binding proteins such as calprotectin, and the metabolic adaptations that support infection.

impact.headline: Making metal withholding visible at the site of infection
impact.discovery: Skaar and collaborators demonstrated that calprotectin accumulates in staphylococcal abscesses and restricts nutrient metals there. Their animal work connected the chemistry of the infected tissue to bacterial growth, helping establish manganese and zinc sequestration as components of nutritional immunity alongside iron restriction.
impact.significance: For microbial metallomics, this changes the unit of analysis: the relevant environment is the metal pool a microbe encounters inside a particular tissue. It makes metal trafficking a concrete antimicrobial research target and gives metal measurements a direct connection to host defense.
impact.frontier: The translational question is which microbial metal dependencies remain vulnerable in human infection while preserving host metal requirements and the functions of beneficial communities.

sources.label: Corbin et al. — Metal chelation and inhibition of bacterial growth in tissue abscesses
Skaar laboratory — Research mission

name: Walter J. Chazin
role: Professor of Biochemistry & Chemistry; Chancellor’s Chair in Medicine
bio: Uses structural biology and biophysics to connect protein structure, dynamics and function. His metal-biology work includes the host-defense protein calprotectin and the molecular basis of antimicrobial metal sequestration.
affiliation: Vanderbilt University · Nashville, USA
bioParagraphs: Uses structural biology and biophysics to connect protein structure, dynamics and function. His metal-biology work includes the host-defense protein calprotectin and the molecular basis of antimicrobial metal sequestration.

impact.headline: Explaining how an immune protein captures a metal
impact.discovery: Chazin and colleagues resolved the molecular basis of manganese sequestration by calprotectin, linking its unusual metal-binding architecture to antimicrobial activity. This structural work explains how a host protein can compete for a nutrient that microbes need, rather than treating calprotectin only as a marker of inflammation.
impact.significance: His contribution gives nutritional immunity a chemical mechanism that can be measured and challenged. For this field, a protein concentration alone is insufficient: its binding sites, metal occupancy and surrounding chemistry determine whether it actually changes the metal available to microbes.
impact.frontier: An important next step is to connect these molecular binding properties to the metal species and protein states present in individual human tissues during inflammation.

sources.label: Damo et al. — Molecular basis for manganese sequestration by calprotectin

name: Thomas E. Kehl-Fie
bio: Investigates how host-imposed nutrient starvation changes bacterial infection. His laboratory studies adaptations that allow Staphylococcus aureus to overcome metal restriction, and how nutritional immunity changes susceptibility to host defenses and antibiotics.
affiliation: University of Iowa · Iowa City, USA
bioParagraphs: Investigates how host-imposed nutrient starvation changes bacterial infection. His laboratory studies adaptations that allow Staphylococcus aureus to overcome metal restriction, and how nutritional immunity changes susceptibility to host defenses and antibiotics.

impact.headline: Showing why metal starvation can change antibiotic performance
impact.discovery: Kehl-Fie’s research connects host-imposed metal starvation to bacterial physiology. In a collaborative 2026 study, calprotectin-mediated zinc restriction reduced β-lactam killing of Staphylococcus aureus in laboratory and mouse experiments. This linked an immune defense to antibiotic tolerance, distinct from inherited antibiotic resistance.
impact.significance: This is a consequential complication for antimicrobial development: an intervention that restricts an essential nutrient may have different effects on bacterial growth and antibiotic killing. Microbial metallomics therefore helps explain why the host environment belongs in the assessment of a proposed treatment.
impact.frontier: The clinical question is whether local metal availability helps explain treatment outcomes in people, and how that information can improve therapy without undermining nutritional immunity.

sources.label: Velez et al. — Calprotectin and β-lactam bactericidal activity
University of Iowa — Understanding how starvation shapes infection

name: Michael D. L. Johnson
bio: Investigates how bacteria process, sense and maintain metals during infection. His laboratory connects microbial metal homeostasis with the host environment and potential antibacterial strategies, including the response of Streptococcus pneumoniae to copper.
affiliation: University of Arizona · Tucson, USA
bioParagraphs: Investigates how bacteria process, sense and maintain metals during infection. His laboratory connects microbial metal homeostasis with the host environment and potential antibacterial strategies, including the response of Streptococcus pneumoniae to copper.

impact.headline: Connecting copper toxicity to a specific metabolic failure
impact.discovery: Johnson and collaborators showed that excess copper disrupts aerobic nucleotide synthesis in Streptococcus pneumoniae, with evidence pointing to interference with a manganese-dependent pathway. The work separated this effect from a general oxidative-stress explanation and proposed mismetallation as a mechanism requiring further resolution.
impact.significance: This makes metal toxicity a question of molecular function, not simply how much copper is present. For microbial metallomics, identifying the failed pathway is what can connect metal competition to microbial behavior and distinguish a plausible antibacterial mechanism from indiscriminate toxicity.
impact.frontier: The next challenge is to establish which metal–protein interactions dominate in relevant host environments and whether they can be targeted with acceptable selectivity and safety.

sources.label: Johnson, Kehl-Fie and Rosch — Copper intoxication and aerobic nucleotide synthesis
University of Arizona — Johnson research profile

name: Elizabeth M. Nolan
bio: Investigates the chemical competition for metals between hosts and microbes. Her work examines antimicrobial metal sequestration by calprotectin, bacterial siderophores and metallophores, and strategies for using iron-acquisition pathways to deliver antibiotics.
affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology · Cambridge, USA
bioParagraphs: Investigates the chemical competition for metals between hosts and microbes. Her work examines antimicrobial metal sequestration by calprotectin, bacterial siderophores and metallophores, and strategies for using iron-acquisition pathways to deliver antibiotics.

impact.headline: Expanding nutritional immunity from metal names to chemical forms
impact.discovery: Nolan’s group demonstrated that calprotectin can sequester ferrous iron and that this iron restriction contributes to bacterial growth inhibition. By identifying an unusual iron-binding site and its chemical behavior, the work expanded a protein chiefly associated with zinc and manganese withholding into a broader metal-defense mechanism.
impact.significance: Her contribution explains why oxidation state and binding chemistry belong in microbiome medicine. An iron measurement does not establish which iron pool a host protein can capture or a microbe can use. That distinction connects coordination chemistry to competition at the host–microbe interface.
impact.frontier: The frontier is to determine when this chemistry controls microbial access in human tissues, and how metal-acquisition pathways might support selective antimicrobial delivery.

sources.label: Nakashige et al. — Human calprotectin is an iron-sequestering host-defense protein

name: Dianne K. Newman
role: Binder/Amgen Professor of Biology and Geobiology; Merkin Institute Professor
bio: Studies bioenergetics and the cell biology of metabolically diverse bacteria. Her work links electron transfer and redox-active metabolites with microbial communities, including biofilms in chronic infections and crop rhizospheres.
affiliation: California Institute of Technology · Pasadena, USA
bioParagraphs: Studies bioenergetics and the cell biology of metabolically diverse bacteria. Her work links electron transfer and redox-active metabolites with microbial communities, including biofilms in chronic infections and crop rhizospheres.

impact.headline: Connecting mineral chemistry to the physiology of biofilms
impact.discovery: Newman’s work connects microbial electron transfer with both environmental mineral transformations and chronic-infection biofilms. Her group showed that a redox-active phenazine can alter iron availability and support biofilm development in laboratory models, linking the chemical state of iron to collective microbial behavior.
impact.significance: This brings a geobiological insight into medicine: microbes can modify the chemistry that governs their own access to resources. A contaminated environment or infected tissue is therefore an active reaction system, and its oxygen conditions and microbial metabolites can matter alongside total metal abundance.
impact.frontier: Translation requires establishing which redox processes are active in patient biofilms and whether changing those processes improves outcomes while protecting host tissue and microbial ecology.

name: Kenneth H. Nealson
bio: Studies microbial physiology, environmental microbiology and the genomics of natural populations. His foundational work on metal-reducing bacteria helped establish Shewanella as a model for extracellular electron transfer and microbial fuel cells.
affiliation: University of Southern California · Los Angeles, USA
bioParagraphs: Studies microbial physiology, environmental microbiology and the genomics of natural populations. His foundational work on metal-reducing bacteria helped establish Shewanella as a model for extracellular electron transfer and microbial fuel cells.

impact.headline: Establishing that microbes can grow by reducing metal minerals
impact.discovery: Myers and Nealson demonstrated microbial growth coupled to manganese-oxide reduction in the organism now known as Shewanella oneidensis MR-1. This foundational work showed that a solid metal oxide can participate directly in microbial energy metabolism, helping make metal-reducing bacteria central models in environmental microbiology.
impact.significance: The importance is broader than an unusual metabolic trait: microorganisms can change the chemical conditions that govern metal mobility and exposure. His work helps explain why predicting contamination requires attention to biological activity, and why some metals are microbial respiratory resources as well as nutrients or toxicants.
impact.frontier: The continuing challenge is to predict when metal-transforming activity in complex environments increases mobility, promotes immobilization, or changes exposure to organisms downstream in the ecosystem.

name: Jeffrey A. Gralnick
bio: Investigates extracellular electron transfer in Shewanella and related microbes. Work on secreted flavins, electron-transfer machinery and bacterial physiology connects basic microbial metabolism with metal reduction and applied biotechnology.
affiliation: University of Minnesota · St. Paul, USA
bioParagraphs: Investigates extracellular electron transfer in Shewanella and related microbes. Work on secreted flavins, electron-transfer machinery and bacterial physiology connects basic microbial metabolism with metal reduction and applied biotechnology.

impact.headline: Revealing the molecules that connect microbes to external metals
impact.discovery: Gralnick and collaborators demonstrated that Shewanella releases flavins that mediate extracellular electron transfer. Subsequent work connected this activity to the organism’s respiratory machinery. These studies explain how microbial metabolism can reach beyond the cell and affect external minerals or conductive surfaces.
impact.significance: For microbial metallomics, this supplies a mechanism between a microbe’s presence and a change in metal chemistry. It also shows why extracellular metabolites belong in measurements of microbial metal handling: interactions can occur through mobile molecules rather than requiring every cell to touch a mineral.
impact.frontier: The next measurement problem is to determine which extracellular pathways carry meaningful electron flow in mixed communities and how that activity changes metal fate under environmental conditions.

name: Derek R. Lovley
bio: Studies the physiology and ecology of anaerobic microorganisms. Work on Geobacter and extracellular electron transfer connects metal reduction with groundwater bioremediation, microbial fuel cells and the development of biological electronic materials.
affiliation: University of Massachusetts Amherst · Amherst, USA
bioParagraphs: Studies the physiology and ecology of anaerobic microorganisms. Work on Geobacter and extracellular electron transfer connects metal reduction with groundwater bioremediation, microbial fuel cells and the development of biological electronic materials.

impact.headline: Showing that microbial metabolism can immobilize a contaminant
impact.discovery: Lovley and colleagues demonstrated that iron-reducing microorganisms can obtain energy through uranium reduction, converting soluble oxidized uranium into a less soluble reduced form. His wider work on Geobacter connects anaerobic metabolism and extracellular electron transfer to the movement and retention of metals in contaminated environments.
impact.significance: This is a foundation for considering microbes as determinants of exposure, not merely organisms damaged by it. His contribution gives bioremediation a mechanistic basis: a microbial community can alter a contaminant’s chemical form and mobility, potentially changing what reaches water supplies and other biological systems.
impact.frontier: The practical frontier is durable containment: establishing whether a reduced metal remains immobilized as oxygen, hydrology and community activity change over time at a contaminated site.

name: Gemma Reguera
role: Professor; Associate Dean for Faculty Affairs and Development
bio: Studies how microbes adapt to environmental change and applies that knowledge to bioremediation, bioenergy and nanotechnology. Her group investigates electroactive microbes, microbial communities that remove agrochemicals, and the behavior of human-associated microbiomes.
affiliation: Michigan State University · East Lansing, USA
bioParagraphs: Studies how microbes adapt to environmental change and applies that knowledge to bioremediation, bioenergy and nanotechnology. Her group investigates electroactive microbes, microbial communities that remove agrochemicals, and the behavior of human-associated microbiomes.

impact.headline: Explaining how contaminant removal and microbial survival connect
impact.discovery: Reguera’s group linked extracellular uranium reduction in Geobacter to protection of the bacterial cell. Their work found that uranium immobilization outside the cell was associated with preserved respiratory activity and viability, connecting the location of a metal transformation to the organism’s ability to sustain that transformation.
impact.significance: Her contribution makes bioremediation a biological performance question as well as a chemical one. A community must keep functioning while it encounters a contaminant. For microbial metallomics, the location of metal deposition and the physiology of participating cells help explain whether removal can continue.
impact.frontier: The next question is how these protective processes operate in heterogeneous field communities and whether contaminant immobilization remains effective as environmental conditions change over time.

sources.label: Cologgi et al. — Extracellular uranium reduction as a protective cellular mechanism

name: Joseph A. Caruso
role: Distinguished Research Professor; Director, Metallomics Center of the Americas
bio: Advanced elemental speciation and ICP-MS-based metallomics through analytical methods that connect chromatography with mass spectrometry. His work helped make it possible to ask which chemical forms of metals occur in biological samples, rather than measuring total elemental abundance alone.
affiliation: University of Cincinnati · Cincinnati, USA
bioParagraphs: Advanced elemental speciation and ICP-MS-based metallomics through analytical methods that connect chromatography with mass spectrometry. His work helped make it possible to ask which chemical forms of metals occur in biological samples, rather than measuring total elemental abundance alone.

impact.headline: Making metal speciation an analytical discipline
impact.discovery: Caruso advanced the coupling of chemical separations with element-sensitive mass spectrometry, including influential work on arsenic and selenium species. He also helped establish the journal Metallomics. His contribution supplied both analytical methods and a scholarly home for studying the biological meaning of particular metal-containing compounds.
impact.significance: Total elemental content cannot reveal every difference between a nutrient, a transformed metabolite and a toxic species. Caruso’s legacy helps make those differences experimentally accessible, providing part of the measurement foundation needed to evaluate foods, microbial transformations and exposure claims in this field.
impact.frontier: The continuing task is reliable speciation in complex samples: preserving compounds during analysis, quantifying recovery and showing which measured species are relevant to biological exposure.

sources.label: RSC — Joseph Anthony Caruso: scientific and editorial contributions

name: Ryszard Łobiński
bio: Develops analytical approaches for detecting, identifying and quantifying trace-metal species in biological and environmental systems. His work helped establish metallomics and links mass spectrometry, chemical speciation and systems microbiology.
affiliation: CNRS / University of Pau · Pau, France
bioParagraphs: Develops analytical approaches for detecting, identifying and quantifying trace-metal species in biological and environmental systems. His work helped establish metallomics and links mass spectrometry, chemical speciation and systems microbiology.

impact.headline: Turning an elemental signal into an identified biological compound
impact.discovery: Łobiński has developed analytical approaches that combine element-specific detection with molecular mass spectrometry. Work identifying previously unknown selenium metabolites in enriched yeast illustrates the contribution: finding selenium in a sample becomes a starting point for determining which molecules contain it and how microbial metabolism has transformed it.
impact.significance: This gives microbial metallomics a way to test claims about chemical form. It is especially relevant when foods or supplements contain products of microbial metabolism: the same total amount of an element can be distributed among different compounds that require separate identification and biological evaluation.
impact.frontier: The frontier is to improve identification and quantification across the full sample while retaining evidence about which compounds survive digestion, enter tissues or remain accessible to microbes.

sources.label: Dernovics, Far and Łobiński — Identification of anionic selenium species in selenium-rich yeast

name: Joanna Szpunar
role: FTMS Bio platform lead, IPREM / UPPA
bio: Develops high-resolution mass-spectrometry approaches for metal, metalloid and biomolecule speciation. The FTMS Bio platform she leads applies Fourier-transform mass spectrometry to environmental and health questions, including molecular identification and quantitative analysis.
affiliation: CNRS / University of Pau · Pau, France
bioParagraphs: Develops high-resolution mass-spectrometry approaches for metal, metalloid and biomolecule speciation. The FTMS Bio platform she leads applies Fourier-transform mass spectrometry to environmental and health questions, including molecular identification and quantitative analysis.

impact.headline: Making the composition of microbial nutrient products testable
impact.discovery: Szpunar’s analytical work distinguishes selenium-containing proteins, metabolites and inorganic forms in enriched yeast. A study with Bierla and Łobiński developed quantification of protein-associated selenocysteine alongside other selenium pools, addressing the problem of assigning an element accurately among the compounds present in a microbial product.
impact.significance: This is directly useful for evaluating what a microbial food or supplement actually contains. It replaces an undifferentiated selenium claim with chemical evidence and supports meaningful comparisons between products, preparations and studies before those differences are interpreted as differences in bioavailability or health effects.
impact.frontier: The next step is to connect well-characterized product composition to transformations during digestion and to measured host and microbial outcomes, rather than assuming composition alone predicts benefit.

name: Uwe Karst
bio: Develops analytical methods for metal speciation and chemical imaging of biological tissues. His group combines laser-ablation ICP-MS, electrochemistry and mass spectrometry to investigate the distribution and transformation of metals and metal-containing compounds.
affiliation: University of Münster · Münster, Germany
bioParagraphs: Develops analytical methods for metal speciation and chemical imaging of biological tissues. His group combines laser-ablation ICP-MS, electrochemistry and mass spectrometry to investigate the distribution and transformation of metals and metal-containing compounds.

impact.headline: Joining the questions of where a metal is and what form it takes
impact.discovery: Karst develops methods for chemical imaging and elemental speciation, combining complementary approaches to map elements and identify metal-containing compounds. His group’s work includes biological tissues and the environmental fate of medical contrast agents, connecting spatial distribution with chemical identity rather than relying on a bulk measurement alone.
impact.significance: For microbial metallomics, these are the tools needed to investigate local exposure. A whole-tissue average can hide a concentrated interface or redistribution between compartments. Imaging and speciation offer different pieces of that problem, helping distinguish where an element accumulates from what it may be doing there.
impact.frontier: The frontier is to align elemental maps with microbial location and molecular identity while controlling sample-preparation artifacts, so apparent colocalization can be tested as a functional interaction.

sources.label: University of Münster — Karst research: imaging and speciation

name: Detlef Günther
role: Professor of Trace Element & Micro Analysis
bio: A leading developer of laser-ablation ICP-MS instrumentation and imaging methods that underpin spatially resolved elemental and metallomic analysis.
affiliation: ETH Zurich · Zurich, Switzerland
bioParagraphs: A leading developer of laser-ablation ICP-MS instrumentation and imaging methods that underpin spatially resolved elemental and metallomic analysis.

impact.headline: Building the instruments that make local metal distributions measurable
impact.discovery: Günther’s research advances laser-ablation ICP-MS and related approaches for trace-element analysis. His work on sample introduction, particle behavior and detection supports spatially resolved multielement measurements, addressing the instrumental limitations that determine whether a small metal-rich region can be distinguished from its surrounding material.
impact.significance: This enables the field to ask where metals are distributed within a sample instead of collapsing everything into one average. For microbial metallomics, such capabilities can support studies of heterogeneous tissues, biofilms and environmental materials, provided the elemental maps are connected to appropriate biological measurements.
impact.frontier: The next challenge is quantitative comparability across sample types and laboratories, together with the spatial resolution and biological registration needed to interpret a measured metal distribution.

name: Manuela Raffatellu
bio: Studies the competition between intestinal pathogens and the microbiota. Her research connects Salmonella colonization, inflammation and nutrient acquisition, including the ways host iron- and metal-withholding defenses reshape microbial competition in the gut.
affiliation: University of California San Diego · La Jolla, USA
bioParagraphs: Studies the competition between intestinal pathogens and the microbiota. Her research connects Salmonella colonization, inflammation and nutrient acquisition, including the ways host iron- and metal-withholding defenses reshape microbial competition in the gut.

impact.headline: Showing how nutritional immunity reshapes competition in the gut
impact.discovery: Raffatellu and collaborators demonstrated that calprotectin-driven zinc restriction can favor Salmonella over competing gut microbes in an inflamed mouse intestine. Her laboratory also studies competition for iron and other nutrients, connecting the host response to the relative success of pathogens and resident community members.
impact.significance: This supplies a crucial ecological correction to the idea that withholding a metal affects all microbes equally. The outcome depends on which organisms can still acquire it. Her work makes community competition central to evaluating nutritional immunity and proposed interventions that alter microbial metal access.
impact.frontier: The translational question is whether metal-dependent competition can be shifted reproducibly in human communities, with benefits demonstrated beyond a change in the abundance of a selected microbe.

name: Andreas J. Bäumler
bio: Studies the ecological and metabolic mechanisms that allow enteric pathogens to colonize the intestine. His work connects inflammation, nutrient availability and bacterial competition, helping explain why Salmonella and related organisms can expand when gut conditions change.
affiliation: University of California Davis · Davis, USA
bioParagraphs: Studies the ecological and metabolic mechanisms that allow enteric pathogens to colonize the intestine. His work connects inflammation, nutrient availability and bacterial competition, helping explain why Salmonella and related organisms can expand when gut conditions change.

impact.headline: Explaining how inflammation changes the microbial habitat
impact.discovery: Bäumler’s work established mechanisms through which intestinal inflammation changes microbial competition, including altered respiratory resources and host nutrient-withholding responses. This connected pathogen expansion to changes in the gut environment itself, rather than explaining dysbiosis only through the presence or absence of particular bacterial species.
impact.significance: His contribution gives microbial metallomics an ecological framework: metal access operates inside a habitat whose oxygen, electron acceptors and nutrients also change. It helps investigators avoid assigning a community shift to a metal alone when the same inflammatory process has changed several resources at once.
impact.frontier: The frontier is to separate these interacting environmental drivers in human disease and determine which changes sustain dysbiosis, rather than merely accompanying the inflammatory response.

name: Karen Pendergrass
bio: Karen Pendergrass investigates upstream metal contamination in food systems and agricultural inputs, and how these exposures may influence microbial metabolism and disease. Her work connects exposure pathways with mismetallation and metal-dependent enzyme function, with particular attention to nickel, urease, [NiFe]-hydrogenases, and nickel-dependent forms of glyoxalase I. By examining microbiome and metallomic signatures together, she explores how changes in metal availability and enzyme activity may link microbial communities and heavy-metal exposure to conditions such as endometriosis and Parkinson’s disease.
affiliation: Microbiome Medicine · Heavy Metal Index · Wikibiome · Institute of Contaminant Standards (ICS)

bioParagraphs: Karen Pendergrass investigates upstream metal contamination in food systems and agricultural inputs, and how these exposures may influence microbial metabolism and disease. Her work connects exposure pathways with mismetallation and metal-dependent enzyme function, with particular attention to nickel, urease, [NiFe]-hydrogenases, and nickel-dependent forms of glyoxalase I. By examining microbiome and metallomic signatures together, she explores how changes in metal availability and enzyme activity may link microbial communities and heavy-metal exposure to conditions such as endometriosis and Parkinson’s disease.

She founded Microbiome Medicine and WikiBiome, is the architect of the Heavy Metal Index, and is founder and standards architect of the Institute of Contaminant Standards (ICS). Her linked institutional and author records describe these roles.

impact.headline: Heavy metals, microbes & microbiome medicine
impact.discovery: Pendergrass develops research frameworks that connect heavy metal exposure, metal-dependent microbial functions, and disease-associated microbiome signatures. Her 2025 Beneficial Microbes Conference presentation examined these connections in endometriosis through metallomics and nutritional immunity. Her subsequent writing applies related questions to Parkinson’s disease, metabolic health, and early-life exposure. Alongside this hypothesis-driven work, she designed the Heavy Metal Index’s evidence architecture and contributes to contaminant standards at ICS.
impact.significance: Microbial metallomics asks what a metal does within a living system, rather than stopping at its measured concentration. Pendergrass’s contribution is to connect that question with both microbial-signature research and traceable exposure evidence. A food contaminant, a microbial enzyme, and a disease-associated community pattern can then be examined as parts of a proposed causal chain. The result is a set of specific mechanisms and research questions, with exposure standards grounded in a separately documented evidence base.
impact.frontier: The next question is which measured changes in metal form and availability explain microbial function in a particular tissue or community. Pairing exposure measurements with enzyme activity and microbiome data would help distinguish a causal metal–microbe relationship from an association, and identify which predictions from these frameworks hold up in independent studies.

portraitAlt: Karen Pendergrass, founder of Microbiome Medicine
profileIntro: Karen Pendergrass is a microbial metallomics researcher, standards architect, and founder of Microbiome Medicine. Her work connects heavy metal exposure with microbes: how a metal reaches a microbial community, which organisms can use or tolerate it, and how those interactions may help explain disease-associated microbiome patterns.

She brings together research on metal-dependent microbial functions, the Heavy Metal Index’s organization of contamination evidence, and standards development at the Institute of Contaminant Standards. This profile connects those projects with her published frameworks, conference presentation, and writing on heavy metals and the microbiome.

name: Divine Aleru
affiliation: Microbiome Medicine (2025–2026) · Bioconductor / BugSigDB (Outreachy)
bio: Divine Aleru translates microbiome research into structured evidence and accessible scientific writing. Her work centers on the interpretation of microbial signatures, study design and disease context, helping readers compare findings across studies and understand what the evidence can support.
bioParagraphs: Divine Aleru translates microbiome research into structured evidence and accessible scientific writing. Her work centers on the interpretation of microbial signatures, study design and disease context, helping readers compare findings across studies and understand what the evidence can support.

As Microbiome Research Coordinator at Microbiome Medicine (2025–2026), she developed and published more than 300 research pages across 15 disease areas, critically appraised clinical and microbiome studies, and wrote research reviews for specialist and non-specialist audiences.

Through Bioconductor’s Outreachy program, she curated more than 100 peer-reviewed studies for BugSigDB, reviewed over 200 studies to improve curation accuracy, and contributed to R tools for analyzing and reporting microbial-signature data. She subsequently served as an Outreachy co-mentor. Her laboratory experience at the University of Chester includes mammalian cell culture and Human Tissue Act training.

impact.headline: Making microbial signatures comparable across studies
impact.discovery: Aleru contributes to BugSigDB’s organization of published microbiome signatures through Bioconductor’s Outreachy program. Her project account describes curation of glucose-metabolism studies and contributions to R-based analysis. This work helps turn scattered findings into structured records that retain information about the study, condition and microbial pattern.
impact.significance: Comparing microbiome and metallomic signatures first requires knowing whether the microbial patterns are comparable at all. Curation provides that foundation: it makes differences in body site, population and study context visible, helping future metal-focused analyses avoid treating every reported association as the same biological signal.
impact.frontier: The next step is to connect curated signatures to measured exposures and microbial functions while keeping association, mechanistic interpretation and clinical validation explicitly separate.

bio: Co-founder of ICS and a member of its executive leadership, with a public record as a co-author of certification standards. Her Microbiome Medicine profile describes a professional nursing background. She is a co-author on research records featured in this guide.

impact.headline: Connecting evidence communication with accountable standards work
impact.discovery: Eyer’s documented contributions combine certification-standard co-authorship and institutional leadership with research curation and writing at Microbiome Medicine. Her public profile describes a nursing background. This places her contribution at the interface of evidence communication and practical standards, where research findings must be translated into clear, documented requirements.
impact.significance: Microbial metallomics needs people who can make complex findings understandable and preserve the distinction between an observation, a proposed explanation and an actionable standard. This work can help audiences follow the evidence while making responsibility for institutional claims and certification decisions visible.
impact.frontier: The next translation task is to show how a standard’s requirements follow from evidence, how uncertainty is handled and whether implementation produces the intended measurable outcomes.
